std.lead: Give&Grow International is a Colombian non-profit entity running two things today: a giving hub with documentary traceability, and a structural triage of homes after the earthquake of 10 August 2026. This page gathers what an institutional partner needs to verify before working with us — including the gaps we are still closing.
std.ident: Legal identity, governance and public documents
std.chs.t: The nine commitments, one by one
std.chs.p: The Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability is the framework an organisation responding to an emergency is measured against. What follows is where we stand on each commitment, with what can be checked and without rounding up.
std.chs.c1.p: The triage is ordered by severity, not by arrival, and every classification is signed by an engineer whose licence has been verified. What gets delivered on the ground is decided by the partner foundation that is there, not by us from Medellín.
std.chs.c2.p: We do not promise dates because we do not have them: the engineers are volunteers and there are fewer of them than there are homes. What we do give, on each family's own screen, is the checkable figure — how many days they have been waiting and how many cases are still unopened.
std.chs.c3.p: We do not rule on whether a home is habitable: that power belongs to the municipal authority under Colombia's Law 1523 of 2012, and overstepping it would be the harm. Programmes are run by local foundations and the credit is theirs, under their own name.
std.chs.c4.p: Every family gets a private link showing where their case stands, and can add material when asked. And we publish what they will NOT receive as prominently as what they will: there is no small print at the end.
std.chs.c5.p: Today only the data-protection route to Colombia's Superintendency of Industry and Commerce exists. The general mechanism, with a confidential route kept separate from the ordinary one, is drafted and awaiting adoption by the highest governing body set out in the bylaws, which today is the founder: the Foundation does not yet have a board.
std.chs.c6.p: We work with verified partner foundations and refer to the municipal authority what belongs to it. We do not yet take part in formal humanitarian coordination mechanisms.
std.chs.c7.p: The system records the cases an engineer could not assess and what material was missing, and that feeds back into what the next family is asked for. There is no external evaluation cycle yet.
std.chs.c8.p: Each engineer's licence is verified by hand in COPNIA's public register. It is the project's only filter and we do not want it automated. The code of conduct is drafted and awaiting adoption by the highest governing body set out in the bylaws (today, the founder).
std.chs.c9.p: No volunteer receives or holds money: every gift arrives through a payment gateway or a bank account in the Foundation's name, generates a tracking number, and its delivery is documented with a record signed by whoever receives it. The donation certificate is signed by the Legal Representative and the Statutory Auditor under oath.
std.chs.nota: No commitment appears here as met unless we can show what with. Three are partial and one does not exist yet: saying so is more useful, both to whoever assesses us and to us, than a table entirely in green that would not survive ten minutes of checking.
std.dnh.p: A volunteer engineer looks at photographs of a damaged home and writes whether there are signs not to stay in it, what precautions to take and what materials to repair it with. What they never write is whether the house is habitable.
std.dnh.p2: That ruling has consequences — evacuation, demolition — and in Colombia it belongs to each municipality's authority under Law 1523 of 2012. A private body issuing it remotely would be displacing the one that actually answers for it, and the family would be left holding a piece of paper that protects them from nothing. That is why the distinction is not a footnote: it governs the whole project, down to the names of the database columns, and it is a mandatory checkbox every engineer accepts before seeing their first case.
std.dat.p: Processing is governed by Colombia's Law 1581 of 2012 and Decree 1377 of 2013. Beyond consent, the system is built so that each party sees the minimum:
std.dat.1: The engineer assessing a home does not see the family's name, phone number or address. They are not needed to give the opinion, and the people who do need them in order to visit are the field team.
std.dat.2: The public register of reviewed homes carries no names, no addresses and no photographs: only the area and the priority. And only families who authorised it appear at all.
std.dat.3: Any authorisation can be withdrawn, and withdrawing it forces removal. Photographs of minors carry reinforced protection under Law 1098 of 2006.
std.no.ey: The limits of what we say
std.no.1.p: We publish the 2025 financial statements signed by the Legal Representative and the Statutory Auditor. They are those of a year of incorporation, with no operations: the Foundation began operating in 2026. We do not publish impact figures that are not backed up.
std.no.2.p: We publish only what we can prove with a document. What a third party reports is labelled as reported by a third party, and we do not present it as ours.
std.no.3.p: We are a young foundation, incorporated in 2025. We do not have a decade of programmes or a large team, and we would rather say so than have it noticed.

origen.t: It all began with a ton of food.
origen.p1: After weeks of work, a campaign hit its goal: a ton of food to deliver to a foundation. But on arrival, the foundation had no way to store or distribute it all. Nearly half was lost. Watching that food go to waste —food someone needed just blocks away— left the founder with a question that wouldn’t let go: how do I close the gap between resources and need, with what I have at hand?
origen.p2: That question became a method. Give&Grow International grew out of nearly four years of Juan Sebastián Navarro Osorio’s field work in La Guajira, the Sierra Nevada and the comunas of Medellín, before the Foundation existed. It was constituted by private document on April 11, 2025, registered with the Medellín Chamber of Commerce on May 19, 2025, as a nonprofit (ESAL), and the DIAN qualifies it under the Special Tax Regime. The purpose: to restore trust in the act of giving, with traceability and no opaque intermediaries.

vol.lead: We want whoever arrives to widen their gaze, and the foundation to end up with something it did not have before. Both things, in the same day.
vol.mira.p: We call it MIRA because that is what it is about: widening the gaze. And because the acronym names its four phases — Marco (Frame), Inmersión (Immersion), Reflexión (Reflection) and Anclaje (Anchoring).
vol.mira.obj: Its technical name states it precisely: a methodology for widening the perceptual field through significant experiences.
vol.mira.def.p: The perceptual field is everything a person manages to see as possible — for themselves and for their surroundings. When someone grows up believing certain things are “not for them”, that limit is often not one of ability: it is one of perception. And the same happens on the other side: someone who has never been in a neighbourhood cannot see what already works there.
vol.mira.def.p2: MIRA works right there. It does not give a speech: it designs an experience where the person does something they did not believe possible, and then helps them put it into words. What widens is not the information they hold: it is what they manage to see as possible.
vol.mira.sigla.t: The four phases, letter by letter
vol.f1.q: It opens the field. A field on the defensive admits no new perception: first a safe space is agreed and a challenge that breaks expectation is set.
vol.f2.q: It creates tension. The experience introduces something the current field cannot explain. That discomfort is what forces it to widen — which is why the challenge must be demanding, though reachable.
vol.f3.q: It consolidates. Lived experience becomes perception when it is put into words. Without this phase the experience fades and the field closes again.
vol.f4.q: It anchors. A small, achievable commitment carries the widened gaze into everyday life, so it does not stay in the day that passed.
vol.mira.why.p: Because removing any of them breaks the chain. Without Frame there is no openness. Without Immersion there is nothing new to explain. Without Reflection there is no meaning, only an anecdote. And without Anchoring there is no transfer: the day stays in the day. That is what separates MIRA from a nice field trip.
vol.mira.teo: It is not a new idea: it draws on the psychology of the perceptual field (Combs and Snygg), Bandura's self-efficacy and Kolb's experiential learning cycle. What is ours is applying it both ways.
vol.mira.iv.p: In Impact Journey, two-way is literal. On the way there, a company team goes to a Social Hub foundation and works alongside its community. On the way back, which is the heart of the method, the foundation's children, young people and families come to the company: they see what life is like for the people who work there, what each area does, what each person studied and what path led them to their role.
vol.mira.iv.p2: For someone who has never been inside an office or a plant, seeing that this work exists and how to reach it widens what they believe is possible for themselves. That is the meaningful experience the method is named after. The foundation always accompanies its people on the way back, with the same care as on the way there.
vol.f1.v: You come to learn from someone who knows something you don't.
vol.f1.p: "You are going to solve something you had never tried."
vol.f2.p: A leading role in the challenge, not a spectator's seat.
vol.f3.v: "What did I believe before arriving that I no longer believe?"
vol.f3.p: "What did I discover in myself that I didn't know I had?"
vol.f4.v: What you are going to give back.
vol.f4.p: A small commitment in their own surroundings.
vol.mira.cierre: Two gazes that widen towards each other. That is giving to grow, and growing to give more.

faq.q11: My home was damaged by the earthquake. What do you do?
faq.a11: If the danger is happening NOW — a wall about to fall, a smell of gas, someone trapped — call 123 and your local council: that does not wait. For everything else there is Mira Mi Casa: you upload photos of your home and a licensed volunteer engineer gives you an opinion at a distance, free of charge. They tell you whether there are signs not to stay in the house or in part of it, what precautions to take meanwhile, and which materials to repair it with and in what order.
faq.q12: Will you tell me whether my home is safe to live in?
faq.a12: No, and it is worth knowing why. Photos do not show the foundations, or the ground, or whether that crack is in a load-bearing wall. And the ruling that carries legal effects — evacuate, demolish — belongs to your municipal authority and not to a private party: Colombia's Law 1523 of 2012 sets that. What we do give you is an opinion on what the photos allow us to see. And if we recommend not using part of the house while it is being checked, that is a precaution, not a ruling of uninhabitability.
faq.q13: Will you repair my house or give me the materials?
faq.a13: We cannot commit to that house by house, and we would rather say so than promise something that does not depend on us alone. As a foundation we will try to arrange help for as many homes as we can. What you do receive for certain is the opinion: which materials to repair with and in what order, so you know where to start even if you source them yourself.
faq.a14: There is no date, and promising one would be worse. The engineers are volunteers and the most serious cases are looked at first. What we do give you are two verifiable figures on your link: how many days you have been waiting and how many cases are still unopened. Keep that link: it is where you see how your case is going and where you upload more photos if we ask for them.
faq.q15: I am an engineer. How can I help?
faq.a15: You apply on the “Volunteer engineers” page with your COPNIA licence number. We check it by hand against COPNIA's public register — a person does that, so it is not immediate — and once it is verified, access opens on its own. What you will do is give an opinion at a distance based on photos — staying, precautions, materials and visit priority — never a habitability ruling. You do not see the family's contact details or address: they are not needed to give the opinion.
faq.q1: How do I make a donation?
faq.a1: In the calculator you pick your amount and continue to payment: you pay by card or with the Bancolombia Button through Wompi, Bancolombia's gateway, and come back with your tracking number. If you prefer a bank transfer, the Bancolombia savings account is 31000009221 in the name of Fundación Give&Grow International (NIT 901.948.930-2); report it afterwards on the site: you get your tracking number instantly and upload your proof right there. That beats emailing it, because your gift is registered and traceable from the first minute.
faq.a2: A benefits programme: partner businesses give discounts to active members, from the Sprout tier, and gain visibility as purpose-driven. The network is just starting, so we would rather say it plainly: the businesses that already give a benefit are the ones listed on the programme page, and they are the only ones. It is built for five categories — food, fashion, beauty, wellbeing and dentistry — and they join one at a time. To get the benefit you show your digital card, and the business checks that it is valid by scanning its QR with its own phone or typing the code or your ID number at thegiveandgrowproject.org/verificar.
faq.q3: How does the tax benefit work?
faq.a3: Your donation may entitle you to an income-tax credit equal to 25% of the amount donated (Art. 257, Colombian Tax Code), subject to the Art. 258 cap. Colombian income-tax filers only; it depends on your tax situation and requires the donation certificate. A cash gift must go through the financial system. For example, COP 4,000,000 donated may mean up to COP 1,000,000 less tax. We are not tax advisers: confirm it with your accountant.
faq.a4: Yes. You can contribute from your own craft — health, law, accounting, communications, development, teaching and more — in the field alongside a partner foundation, in the Social Hub's structure, or combining both. Tell us your area and your availability.
faq.q5: Can my foundation apply to the Social Hub?
faq.a5: Yes. We look for foundations and grassroots community projects with verifiable field work and a willingness to embrace traceability. Each one joins with verification and an agreement; if it is a grassroots community project, we say so on its profile. Some partners contribute services to the Social Hub as well as receiving.

faq.a7: Yes. In Memberships you register your card once and it is charged automatically every month. If you choose a one-off gift in Donate, it is processed only once. In every case you receive your receipt with a tracking number once the payment is confirmed. The donation certificate for tax purposes is separate: you request it when you give, it is signed by the Legal Representative and the Statutory Auditor under oath, and a person issues it — which is why we need your ID document and your city.

faq.a6: The Social Hub is not just a channel for giving: it is an operations centre with five routes connecting partnerships, donations and measurable impact. Three things define it. First, traceability: your gift has a tracking number and an automatic receipt; on request, a signed donation certificate; and when the foundation delivers, the signed handover record and its photos appear in your tracking page. Second, evidence rather than promises: we are a young foundation that shows what it can prove, with no inflated figures, and we work with partner foundations verified on the ground. Third, reciprocity: giving helps you grow too — members access the Gratitude Program benefits and companies gain visibility as businesses with purpose. That is what our motto sums up: «Give to grow, grow to give more».

impactos.why.p: The sector's problem is not a lack of generosity: it is that almost no one keeps the record. Without a system, every donation is a one-off favour — impossible to audit, to repeat or to report precisely. ImpactOS exists so that giving no longer depends on someone's memory.

med.lead: The work on the ground belongs to the partner foundation; we amplify it, record it and report it. This page states the evidence we speak from — and where what we can prove ends.
med.contrib.p: Give&Grow does not cause the impact on its own: the foundation does the work in its community. That is why every report is written in terms of contribution. It is the technically correct way, and it is what the motto already says: we do not replace foundations, we amplify them.

med.contrib.note: The difference looks like wording and it is not: in the first sentence the credit stays where the work was done, and the contribution stays verifiable.
med.esc.p: Measuring impact has degrees, and confusing them is the most common mistake in the sector. These are the three, with the real status of each.
med.e1.p: What one real unit of service costs, documented by the foundation that provides it. A meal at Niños del Futuro costs $4,000 COP, and that is where the equivalence in the calculator comes from. It measures what was delivered.
med.e2.p: What changed in people, beyond what was delivered. The MIRA instruments record it in aggregated, anonymous form. Without a professional on the team we observe, we do not diagnose: we issue no individual results and no clinical conclusions.
med.e3.p: We do not publish it, and this is not decorative caution: an SROI is not a calculation, it is a study. It requires financial proxies, a baseline, consultation with stakeholders, and four technical discounts — deadweight, attribution, displacement and drop-off. Without those, a social return ratio falls apart in the first meeting, and everything else that is true falls with it.
med.esc.note: The first rung measures what was delivered; the third would measure the value of the change produced. They are not the same thing. The raw material already exists: ImpactOS records destination, unit, receipt, delivery and report. What is missing is the outcomes layer and the methodological rigour, not the data.
med.pub.p: These rules govern every figure on this site and in any report we sign.
med.pub.1: Always aggregated and anonymous: never an identifiable individual case.
med.pub.2: With recorded consent for any material from the community — photo, testimony or journal.
med.pub.3: With a visible cut-off date: a figure without a date is not evidence.
med.pub.4: With the source stated: which instrument produced it, whether a record, a journey log or an observation.
med.pub.5: Third-party figures are marked as reported, never as our own.
med.pub.6: We prefer recency over cumulative totals: how many journeys and how long ago the last evidence was says more than an unaudited total.
med.pub.7: No social return ratios as long as there is no study to support them.

brig.t: The 10 August earthquake. The brigade set out on 20 August 2026.
brig.lead: A magnitude 7.4 earthquake with its epicentre in Chocó struck the west of the country. On 20 August 2026 the brigade set out for the affected area, to deliver alongside the foundations already working in each territory. This page is the report of what was done: the signed handover records are published in the tracking page once they are ready. What remains open is Mira Mi Casa.
brig.hechos.nota: Casualty and displacement figures change by the hour and are published by the national risk agency (UNGRD). We do not repeat them here: it would mean publishing a number that is false tomorrow.
brig.mmc.t: What comes next is Mira Mi Casa. Moving one house forward takes three different people.
brig.mmc.p: The brigade carried what fits in a truck. What comes next cannot be carried: it is an engineer's opinion on one specific house, and the materials to repair it in the right order. That takes three roles, and each one comes in through its own door.
brig.mmc1.d: They upload photos from a phone, with no account and no password. They get a case number and a private link to see where it stands and add more photos if asked.
brig.mmc2.t: A volunteer engineer gives an opinion.
brig.mmc2.d: They look at those photos and give an opinion at a distance: whether there are signs not to stay in the house or in part of it, what precautions to take meanwhile, and which materials to repair it with and in what order. With a licence verified in COPNIA's public register. They do not declare a house habitable: that belongs to the municipal authority.
brig.mmc3.d: They contribute materials, labour, transport or money for homes that already have an opinion. Nothing is charged online and no specific house is promised: the offer is registered first and then we talk.
brig.mmc.cierre: None of the three works alone: without photos there is no opinion, without an opinion there is no knowing what to buy, and without materials the opinion stays on paper.
brig.plan.p: Collection happened at drop-off points in Envigado hosted by companies and friends. From there the load left with the team, by road, from 20 August 2026.
brig.sec.cap: The five sectors in the plan
brig.sec.nota: Areas and delivery points were agreed with each Municipal Risk Management Council and with the foundations in each territory. What was delivered in each sector, and to how many families, is published with its signed record once reviewed: we do not claim it before then.
brig.hub.t: We do not show up to hand things out on our own.
brig.hub.p: We delivered alongside foundations that already worked in each territory and knew the families: they brought the judgement and the relationship, we brought the logistics, the supplies and the record. It is the same Social Hub model we run all year, applied to an emergency.
brig.nec.p: The inventory had more than a hundred items across thirteen categories, twenty-four of them critical. This is what they grouped, and why.
brig.c1.r: Without a lid, water is recontaminated within hours.
brig.c1.d: Purification tablets, sealed buckets, gravity filters and waste management.
brig.c2.r: Pull-tab cans are mandatory: in an emergency there is no can opener.
brig.c2.d: Canned protein, ready-to-eat pulses, oral rehydration salts and disposable tableware.
brig.c3.r: There are intimate needs nobody asks for out loud.
brig.c3.d: Soap, toilet paper, complete menstrual hygiene kits and new underwear.
brig.c4.r: Always forgotten, and their absence humiliates.
brig.c4.d: Early childhood and older adults: nappies by size, wipes and barrier cream.
brig.c5.r: Sleeping on a sports hall floor is the number one complaint.
brig.c5.d: Insulating mats, mountain-weather blankets, waterproof tarpaulins and ponchos.
brig.c6.r: Talking to your family is not a luxury: it is a humanitarian need.
brig.c6.d: Solar lamps, torches, batteries and power strips that turn one socket into a community charging point.
brig.c7.r: The brigade never consumes what belongs to the families.
brig.c7.d: Helmets, boots, certified masks, institutional ID and the handover records.

cv.aviso: This does not replace a visit or your municipality's ruling. A volunteer engineer looks at your photos and writes what they can tell from them: what precautions to take meanwhile and, when your photos allow it, where it makes sense to start repairing. cv.gestion: We will try to arrange help for every home we can, and we cannot commit to it house by house. We would rather tell you that up front than promise something that does not depend on us alone.
cv.s1.0: If the danger is happening NOW — a wall about to fall, a smell of gas, someone trapped — this is not what you need: call 123 and your local council. An opinion based on photos has no deadline, and an emergency does not wait.
cv.s1.1: Do not go in if you see collapsed walls, sunken roofs or broken columns. Take the photos from outside.
cv.s1.2: Do not climb onto the roof or onto ladders.
cv.s1.3: Do not move rubble to show the damage better.
cv.s1.4: If you smell gas, get out and tell someone. Do not switch anything on.
cv.s1.5: If there are aftershocks, wait. The house will still be there.
cv.s1.fin: Better one photo less than an accident. If something feels unsafe, skip it and just tell us.

ing.t: There are more damaged homes than engineers to visit them.
ing.lead: After the 10 August earthquake, more requests arrive than any field team can handle. We are not asking you to rule from a distance: we are asking you to look at some photos, say whether there are signs not to stay, and what should be repaired and with what.
ing.volver.p: If you have already applied and we verified your licence, this is your door.
ing.q.p: This distinction is not fine print: it governs the whole project, down to the names of the database columns. If you do not share it, this is not the place — and we would rather say so up front.
ing.q1.p: You give an opinion at a distance: whether there are signs not to stay in the house or in part of it, what precautions to take in the meantime, and which materials to repair it with and in what order. And you order the queue: urgent visit, scheduled, none needed for now, or cannot be assessed with this material.
ing.q2.p: You do not declare a home habitable or uninhabitable, and nobody here will ask you to sign that: declarations with legal effects — evacuate, demolish — belong to the municipal authority under Colombia's Law 1523 of 2012. Recommending that part of a house not be used while it is being checked is not declaring it uninhabitable: it is a precaution, and it is written as one.
ing.q3.p: You cannot see the foundation, you cannot see the soil, and you do not know whether that wall is load-bearing. That is why «I cannot assess this» is a first-class answer and not a failure: choosing it forces the system to ask you what is missing, and to request it from the family.
ing.c.t: From application to your first case
ing.p1.p: With your name, your professional licence number and your city. Two minutes.
ing.p2.p: We look it up in COPNIA's public register. A person does this, so it is not instant: it is the only filter the project has and we do not want it automated.
ing.p3.p: With your email address, whichever you prefer — university, company or personal. No account and no password: you request a code, it arrives in your inbox, and you are in.
ing.p4.p: You open a case, see its photos and classify it. You do not see the family's name, phone or address: they are not needed to give the opinion, and the people who do need them to go and visit are the field team.
ing.f.p: The family receives a PDF with your name, your licence number and what you wrote. That is why you review the cases you want and none that you do not, and why asking for more material is always an option. Nothing about this is charged, in either direction.
ing.form.lead: There is no minimum number of cases and no schedule. There is a verification before you start.
ing.email.h: You would sign in with this same address. University, company or personal — it does not matter.
ing.matricula.h: The one on your COPNIA card. It is what we will verify in their public register.
ing.posgrado.h: If you have several, separate them with commas.
ing.diplomados.h: Short and professional-body courses count. If it is about post-earthquake assessment, say so: that carries weight here.

ap.no.2.p: Neither the engineer's opinion nor a repair declares that a home can be lived in. That ruling, with effects such as evacuating or demolishing, belongs to the municipal authority under Colombia's Law 1523 of 2012.

mmc.p.t: Your home, reviewed by an engineer.
mmc.p.lead: Free, and from your phone. You upload photos and a licensed volunteer engineer writes to you: whether there are signs you should not stay in the home or in part of it, what precautions to take and what materials to repair with.
mmc.p.rol.t: Moving one home forward takes three different people
mmc.p.rol.lead: Each one comes in through their own door and none does the other's work.
mmc.p.rol1.p: You upload photos from your phone, with no account and no password. You get a case number and a private link: there you see where your case stands and you can add more photos if you are asked for them. It is free, and no screen will ever ask you for money.
mmc.p.rol2.k: If you are an engineer or architect
mmc.p.rol2.p: You apply with your COPNIA licence and we verify it by hand in their public register. After that you review the cases you want, when you can, and write a remote opinion. You do not see the family's name, phone number or address.
mmc.p.rol3.p: Materials, labour, transport or money for the homes that already have an opinion. You register what you can give and someone from the team writes to you. Nothing is charged online here and no particular home is reserved: the order comes from the engineers' opinions, not from the photos.
mmc.p.rol.cierre: None of the three works alone: without photos there is no opinion, without an opinion nobody knows what to buy, and without materials the opinion stays on paper.
mmc.p.alc.lead: This distinction governs the whole project, so it goes at the entrance and not in small print at the end.
mmc.p.si.p: A written opinion signed by a licensed engineer: whether there are signs not to stay in the home or in part of it, what precautions to take meanwhile, what materials to repair with and in what order, and how urgently a visit is advisable. It arrives at their private link, with the name and licence number of whoever signed it.
mmc.p.no.p: A habitability ruling, which is not ours to give: evacuating or demolishing is decided by each municipality's authority, under Colombia's Law 1523 of 2012. Nor a guaranteed visit, a response date or a promise that their home will be repaired. We will seek to arrange help for every home we can, and we cannot commit to it house by house.
mmc.p.alc.fotos: And there is a limit no engineer can get around: photos do not show the foundations, or the ground, or whether that wall is load-bearing. That is why «I cannot assess this» is a first-class answer in the system, and marking it forces the engineer to say what is missing so we can ask the family for it.
mmc.p.conf.ey: Who we are and who we are not
mmc.p.conf.t: This is free and we are not the government
mmc.p.conf.lead: A new name asking for photos of your home in a disaster zone looks a lot like a scam. So we say it plainly, and tell you how to check.
mmc.p.conf1.t: We will never ask you for money
mmc.p.conf1.p: No fee, no paperwork, no card or bank details. This site charges a family nothing on any screen. If someone asks you for money in the name of Mira Mi Casa, it is not us.
mmc.p.conf2.t: We do not handle housing subsidies
mmc.p.conf2.p: We have no connection to state housing programmes and we do not process official aid. If what you need is a subsidy, the route is your local council. Here we give a technical opinion and look for materials, and that is all we do.
mmc.p.conf3.p: Your name, phone number and address are seen by the team that coordinates the visit and by nobody else: the engineer reviewing your photos does not see them, because they are not needed to give the opinion. In the public record of homes only the neighbourhood appears, and only if you authorised it.
mmc.p.conf.quien: Mira Mi Casa is the platform of Cimientos que Unen, a project of Fundación Give&Grow International: a non-profit entity based in Medellín, tax ID 901.948.930-2. If you arrived under one of those names and landed on another, that is the chain, and not a bait and switch.
mmc.p.conf.link: See the foundation's registration and public documents
mmc.p.pas.t: From a family's phone to an engineer's opinion
mmc.p.pas1.p: A few details, a few photos and two authorisations. At the end you are left with your case number and your private link. Keep it: it is what you come back with.
mmc.p.pas2.p: Not first come, first served: what looks most serious from what you told us —whether anyone was hurt, whether people live there, what the walls are made of— is reviewed first. Your link tells you two things you can check — how many days you have been waiting and how many cases are still unopened.
mmc.p.pas3.p: They look at your photos and write the opinion. If what you sent is not enough, they mark that they cannot assess it and we ask you for exactly what is missing: that is why the link also works for uploading more.
mmc.p.pas4.t: The opinion arrives at your link
mmc.p.pas4.p: With the name and licence number of whoever signed it. From then on your home has something concrete to ask for, and it is what we show to anyone willing to sponsor a repair.
mmc.p.pas.fecha: What you will not find is a promised date. The engineers are volunteers and there are fewer of them than there are homes: we would rather tell you than invent a deadline.
mmc.p.fin.t: What has already been reviewed is published
mmc.p.fin.p: Every reviewed home appears in a public record with no names, no addresses and no photos: only the area and how urgent it is. It is how we prove what we say instead of asking you to take our word for it.

bc.od.t: Download the register and use it
bc.od.p: This register is not only there to be looked at. It downloads in full, in the format the sector works with, and can be reused with attribution. It carries exactly what the table above carries: no names, no addresses, no photographs.
bc.od.d1: caso — the case number. It is public and identifies nobody.
bc.od.d2: sector — the neighbourhood or area the family wrote. It is the only thing that locates the home, and it deliberately goes no finer than that.
bc.od.d3: prioridad — urgente, programada, no_requiere or inevaluable. Written by an engineer whose licence was verified in COPNIA's public register.
bc.od.d4: material_muros — ladrillo, adobe, bahareque, prefabricado, madera or no_se. Empty when the family did not say.
bc.od.d5: pisos — how many storeys, according to the family.
bc.od.d6: reportado_en — when the family reported it, in UTC. Colombia is UTC−5.
bc.od.nota: The CSV uses a semicolon separator and carries a byte order mark, so it opens correctly in Excel with no fiddling. Up to 5,000 records download at once; if there were ever more, the response says so in its headers rather than handing you a short file that looks complete.
bc.od.uso: You may reuse this data, including commercially, citing Fundación Give&Grow International as the source. What we ask in return is what we demand of ourselves: do not claim more with it than it says. A classification is an opinion formed from photographs, not a habitability ruling.
